/*
 * frame_capture.c — Capture MJPEG video from a USB webcam on a Raspberry Pi 4
 * Model B using libgpiod-style mmap-based frame retrieval and select() polling.
 *
 * Build:  gcc -O2 -Wall -Wextra -o frame_capture frame_capture.c
 * Run:    ./frame_capture
 *
 * The program reads frames from /dev/video0, timestamps them, and writes
 * "seconds.microseconds" to frame_log.txt.  It uses select() for non-blocking
 * I/O so that the program can respond to SIGINT promptly.
 */

#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <errno.h>
#include <fcntl.h>
#include <unistd.h>
#include <sys/ioctl.h>
#include <sys/mman.h>
#include <sys/select.h>
#include <time.h>
#include <signal.h>
#include <linux/videodev2.h>

#define DEVICE_NAME "/dev/video0"
#define LOG_FILE "frame_log.txt"
#define MAX_FRAMES 100

/* ---- Per-device state ---- */
typedef struct {
    int fd;
    void *buffer;
    size_t buffer_size;
    int buffer_mapped;
} device_t;

/* ---- Globals for signal-safe cleanup ---- */
static volatile sig_atomic_t g_running = 1;
static device_t g_device;

/* ------------------------------------------------------------------ */
static void signal_handler(int sig)
{
    (void)sig;
    g_running = 0;
}

/* ------------------------------------------------------------------ */
static int xioctl(int fd, unsigned long request, void *arg)
{
    int r;
    do {
        r = ioctl(fd, request, arg);
    } while (r == -1 && errno == EINTR);
    return r;
}

/* ------------------------------------------------------------------ */
static int init_device(device_t *d)
{
    d->fd = open(DEVICE_NAME, O_RDWR);
    if (d->fd < 0) {
        fprintf(stderr, "open(%s): %s\n", DEVICE_NAME, strerror(errno));
        return -1;
    }

    struct v4l2_capability cap;
    if (xioctl(d->fd, VIDIOC_QUERYCAP, &cap) < 0) {
        fprintf(stderr, "VIDIOC_QUERYCAP: %s\n", strerror(errno));
        goto fail;
    }
    if (!(cap.capabilities & V4L2_CAP_VIDEO_CAPTURE)) {
        fprintf(stderr, "%s is not a video capture device\n", DEVICE_NAME);
        goto fail;
    }
    if (!(cap.capabilities & V4L2_CAP_STREAMING)) {
        fprintf(stderr, "%s does not support streaming I/O\n", DEVICE_NAME);
        goto fail;
    }

    struct v4l2_format fmt;
    memset(&fmt, 0, sizeof(fmt));
    fmt.type = V4L2_BUF_TYPE_VIDEO_CAPTURE;
    fmt.fmt.pix.width = 640;
    fmt.fmt.pix.height = 480;
    fmt.fmt.pix.pixelformat = V4L2_PIX_FMT_MJPEG;
    fmt.fmt.pix.field = V4L2_FIELD_NONE;

    if (xioctl(d->fd, VIDIOC_S_FMT, &fmt) < 0) {
        fprintf(stderr, "VIDIOC_S_FMT: %s\n", strerror(errno));
        goto fail;

/*
 * frame_capture.c — Capture MJPEG video from a USB webcam on a Raspberry Pi 4
 * Model B using libgpiod-style mmap-based frame retrieval and select() polling.
 *
 * Build:  gcc -O2 -Wall -Wextra -o frame_capture frame_capture.c
 * Run:    ./frame_capture
 *
 * The program reads frames from /dev/video0, timestamps them, and writes
 * "seconds.microseconds" to frame_log.txt.  It uses select() for non-blocking
 * I/O so that the program can respond to SIGINT promptly.
 */

#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <errno.h>
#include <fcntl.h>
#include <unistd.h>
#include <sys/ioctl.h>

#include <linux/videodev2.h>

#define DEVICE_NAME "/dev/video0"
#define LOG_FILE "frame_log.txt"
#define MAX_FRAMES 100

/* ---- Per-device state ---- */
typedef struct {
    int fd;
    void *buffer;
    size_t buffer_size;
    int buffer_mapped;
} device_t;

/* ---- Globals for signal-safe cleanup ---- */
static volatile sig_atomic_t g_running = 1;
static device_t g_device;

/* ------------------------------------------------------------------ */
static void signal_handler(int sig)
{
    (void)sig;
    g_running = 0;
}

/* ------------------------------------------------------------------ */
static int xioctl(int fd, unsigned long request, void *arg)
{
    int r;
    do {
        r = ioctl(fd, request, arg);
    } while (r == -1 && errno == EINTR);
    return r;
}

/* ------------------------------------------------------------------ */
static int init_device(device_t *d)
{
    d->fd = open(DEVICE_NAME, O_RDWR);
    if (d->fd < 0) {
        fprintf(stderr, "open(%s): %s\n", DEVICE_NAME, strerror(errno));
        return -1;
    }

    struct v4l2_capability cap;
    if (xioctl(d->fd, VIDIOC_QUERYCAP, &cap) < 0) {
        fprintf(stderr, "VIDIOC_QUERYCAP: %s\n", strerror(errno));
        goto fail;
    }
    if (!(cap.capabilities & V4L2_CAP_VIDEO_CAPTURE)) {
        fprintf(stderr, "%s is not a video capture device\n", DEVICE_NAME);
        goto fail;
    }
    if (!(cap.capabilities & V4L2_CAP_STREAMING)) {
        fprintf(stderr, "%s does not support streaming I/O\n", DEVICE_NAME);
        goto fail;
    }

    struct v4l2_format fmt;
    memset(&fmt, 0, sizeof(fmt));
    fmt.type = V4L2_BUF_TYPE_VIDEO_CAPTURE;
    fmt.fmt.pix.width = 640;
    fmt.fmt.pix.height = 480;
    fmt.fmt.pix.pixelformat = V4L2_PIX_FMT_MJPEG;
    fmt.fmt.pix.field = V4L2_FIELD_NONE;

    if (xioctl(d->fd, VIDIOC_S_FMT, &fmt) < 0) {
        fprintf(stderr, "VIDIOC_S_FMT: %s\n", strerror(errno));
        goto fail;

    memset(&parm, 0, sizeof(parm));
    parm.type = V4L2_BUF_TYPE_VIDEO_CAPTURE;

    parm.parm.capture.timeperframe.denominator = 1000; /* 1 ms */

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi that controls a camera pan‑tilt mount using two hobby servos driven over the GPIO hardware PWM bus, with four active‑low push‑buttons wired to ground and using the internal pull‑up resistors; the pan servo is connected to GPIO4 (BCM) and the tilt servo to GPIO5 (BCM), while the UP, DOWN, LEFT and RIGHT buttons are on GPIO6, GPIO7, GPIO8 and GPIO9 respectively, all using 50 Hz PWM where each loop iteration increments the pulse width by 10 µs and the loop delays 50 ms, the pulse widths must be clamped between 1000 µs (minimum) and 2000 µs (maximum) with a center position of 1500 µs, the program must initialize the driver library and check its return value, printing an error and exiting if initialization fails, output a startup message showing the pin assignments and the center position, respond to button presses by adjusting the appropriate servo pulse width in the allowed range, and install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler that cleanly stops PWM on both servo pins using the library's API call, calls the library's API call() to release resources, and then exits.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that monitors an HC‑SR501 PIR sensor connected on the GPIO bus with its output tied to GPIO17 (BCM, physical pin 11), debounces each motion detection for two seconds, and otherwise polls the pin every 100 ms; when motion is detected the program must capture a JPEG snapshot from the Camera Module v2 at quality 85, store the file in a directory named motion_captures (creating the directory if necessary and handling an existing directory gracefully), then compose a JSON payload containing the filename, an ISO 8601 timestamp with microseconds, the motion status, and the GPIO pin number and POST this payload together with the image to an HTTP endpoint at http://<IP>:<port>/upload, where the IP address and port are supplied as command‑line arguments; the program must initialize the sensor driver and the HTTP library, configure GPIO17 as an input with a pull‑down resistor, check and report any initialization, system call, file, or network errors to stderr, and on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM perform a clean shutdown by releasing the driver, performing the required global cleanup of the HTTP library, and exiting, while ensuring the global HTTP library initialization is called exactly once at startup and the corresponding cleanup is called exactly once at exit.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that monitors the HC‑SR501 PIR sensor on the GPIO bus, using the sensor’s output connected to GPIO17 (BCM, physical pin 11) as an input with edge‑falling detection, implements a 50 ms debounce by waiting for a falling edge with a timeout, and upon a valid motion event invokes the camera capture utility with the options ‑o <filename> ‑‑width 640 ‑‑height 480 ‑q 85 ‑‑timeout 2000 ‑‑nopreview to produce a timestamped JPEG saved in /home/pi/images using the filename format YYYYMMDD_HHMMSS_mmm.jpg; each capture and any error from the capture command must be logged with a timestamp to /home/pi/motion_capture.log; the program must open the GPIO chip, claim GPIO17 as an input with edge‑falling (or edge‑rising) detection, check return codes of the capture command and log failures, and handle SIGINT and SIGTERM cleanly by releasing all driver library resources and closing file descriptors, while assuming the images directory already exists and avoiding any network publishing, ZeroMQ, or use of a driver library.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads arrow‑key presses and a ‘q’ character from stdin, uses the GPIO hardware PWM bus to drive two SG90 servo motors—one pan servo attached to GPIO17 (BCM) and one tilt servo attached to GPIO18 (BCM)—operating at a 50 Hz frequency, initializing the driver library and exiting with code 1 after printing an error if initialization fails, starting both servos at a neutral 90‑degree position, moving each servo in 5‑degree steps in response to the appropriate arrow key while enforcing angle limits of 0 to 180 degrees and printing clear error messages for any out‑of‑range angle or PWM failure, inserting a 100 ms delay between successive commands, and handling cleanup by setting both servos to neutral, terminating the driver library cleanly, and exiting when a SIGINT signal is received or the user presses ‘q’.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads the CPU temperature from /sys/class/thermal/thermal_zone0/temp and parses the CPU usage percentage from /proc/stat, then renders both values once per second on an SSD1306 128×64 I2C OLED display attached to I2C bus 1, using a basic 5×7 bitmap font for text; the program must check every I2C write operation for errors, handle file‑read failures by returning specific error strings to be shown on the OLED, log any I2C communication failures to stderr and exit gracefully, and install a SIGINT handler to cleanly release all resources before termination.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads the pulse output of a YF‑S201 water flow sensor connected to GPIO17 (BCM numbering), computes the instantaneous flow rate and accumulates total volume, logs the current flow rate and total volume to the console once every second, and updates an HD44780 LCD attached via I2C bus 1 every ten seconds to display the same current flow rate and accumulated volume; the implementation must include robust error handling for any failures during GPIO initialization and must anticipate and manage possible I2C communication errors, and it must also catch SIGINT and SIGTERM signals to perform a graceful shutdown that releases all GPIO and I2C resources.

/*
 * YF-S201 Water Flow Sensor Reader with HD44780 LCD Display
 * Board:  Raspberry Pi 4 Model B
 * Sensor: YF-S201 pulse output on GPIO17 (BCM)
 * LCD:    HD44780 on I2C bus 1, address 0x27
 *
 * Build:  gcc -O2 -Wall -o flow_monitor flow_monitor.c -lpigpio -lrt
 * Run:    sudo ./flow_monitor
 */

#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <stdint.h>
#include <stdbool.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <errno.h>
#include <signal.h>
#include <time.h>
#include <unistd.h>
#include <pigpio.h>

/* ----------------------------- Configuration ----------------------------- */
#define FLOW_SENSOR_GPIO      17          /* BCM pin for YF-S201 pulse output */
#define LCD_I2C_BUS           1           /* I2C bus number (Raspberry Pi 4) */
#define LCD_I2C_ADDR          0x27        /* HD44780 default I2C address     */
#define LCD_COLS              16          /* Number of columns on HD44780 */
#define LCD_ROWS              2           /* Number of rows on HD44780    */
#define LCD_CHR               1           /* HD44780 data mode         */
#define LCD_CMD               0           /* HD44780 command mode       */

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that communicates with an Omron B5L‑LD50‑07050 3D TOF sensor over the I2C bus (/dev/i2c-1) to detect intrusion events within 1 meter and log the average distance; the program must send the documented 4‑byte command frame to request a measurement, wait at least 10 ms before reading the documented 15‑byte response, verify that byte 0 matches the documented header value, extract the 16‑bit big‑endian distance from bytes 11 and 12, sample the sensor ten times per cycle with a 100 ms delay between cycles, compute the average distance, and when the average is less than 1000 mm write a timestamp and the average distance to a file named intrusion_log.txt; all I2C open, ioctl, read and write calls must be checked for failure, and the code must gracefully handle sensor‑absent (I2C NACK) and bus‑error conditions, while also installing a SIGINT handler so that pressing Ctrl‑C closes the I2C file descriptor and any open log files and releases all resources on every exit path.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the I2C bus 1 to periodically read the distance from an Adafruit VL53L0X Time‑of‑Flight sensor, verifying the sensor’s presence at startup by reading its model ID register and confirming it matches the documented value, and exiting cleanly with an error message if the read fails or the ID mismatches; after successful initialization the program must poll the RESULT_INTERRUPT_STATUS with roughly a 100 ms timeout, obtain a distance measurement, and every 500 ms print to stdout a line formatted as “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS Distance: <N> mm”, while checking every I2C call for errors and printing strerror(errno) on failure, issuing a warning to stderr and continuing to the next iteration for any read/write error that occurs during the loop; the program must also handle SIGINT and SIGTERM gracefully by closing the I2C handle, invoking the library’s cleanup call, and exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that periodically reads the 16‑bit proximity data from a Silicon Labs Si1182 optical sensor connected on I2C bus 1 (GPIO2 SDA / GPIO3 SCL) and logs the values to the console every 500 ms, while checking each driver library or I2C call for errors, detecting a sensor‑absent condition by a NACK on the initial write, handling any bus errors gracefully without crashing, and installing a SIGINT handler so that pressing Ctrl +C cleanly closes the I2C handle and invokes the library’s API call() for proper cleanup.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that opens the I2C bus 1 device file (/dev/i2c-1) with full error checking, sets the Melexis MLX75030 Time‑of‑Flight sensor as the I2C slave using ioctl I2C_SLAVE and verifies that the device responds, then enters a loop that every 500 ms (using nanosleep) reads the distance measurement from the sensor and prints a line to stdout in the form “Distance: <value> mm”; if an I2C read fails the program must write a diagnostic message to stderr and simply continue to the next cycle without exiting, while if the sensor is not present at startup it must print an error and exit with status 1; a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler must be installed so that pressing Ctrl‑C cleanly closes the I2C file descriptor and terminates the program with status 0.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that periodically reads the Texas Instruments OPT3101 Time‑of‑Flight sensor on I2C bus 1, logging every 500 ms the distance measurement from channel 0, the ambient light value, and any error flags to the console, while implementing robust error handling for I2C communication failures such as a missing sensor or bus errors and guaranteeing that all resources are cleanly released on every exit path, including a graceful shutdown when a SIGINT (Ctrl‑C) is received.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that periodically reads distance from an HC‑SR04 ultrasonic sensor connected on the GPIO bus, using GPIO 17 (BCM) as the trigger output and GPIO 18 (BCM) as the echo input, issuing a 10 µs trigger pulse each cycle, waiting up to 200 ms for the echo rising edge and up to 200 ms for the echo falling edge, and performing one read per second; each valid measurement must be logged to the console together with a timestamp, while the code must handle driver library initialization failure, echo‑edge timeouts, and invalid pulse durations (≤ 0 µs or > 38 ms, the HC‑SR04 maximum range timeout), include a comment noting that the HC‑SR04 operates at 5 V and the Pi GPIO is only 3.3 V tolerant and therefore a 1 kΩ resistor must be used on the echo line within the library’s API call() that provides microsecond precision, and finally ensure graceful shutdown on SIGINT or SIGTERM by invoking the library’s API call() on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that reads a range profile from a Texas Instruments IWR1443 mmWave radar over UART (/dev/serial0), decodes each data frame marked by an 8‑byte magic word header followed by 128 bytes of raw range profile data representing 64 little‑endian 16‑bit distance bins, checks whether any bin indicates a target within a 1.0‑meter distance threshold, and on detection logs an intrusion entry containing an ISO 8601 timestamp and the distance in meters to a comma‑separated file named intrusion_log.csv, while also activating an alert LED connected to GPIO 17 (BCM) for exactly 2 seconds; the program must handle UART initialization errors using the POSIX driver library, validate all I/O operations, gracefully manage sensor‑absent or bus‑error conditions, and ensure clean release of all resources on every exit path by handling SIGINT and SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously reads obstacle detection data from an E18-D80NK IR sensor connected to GPIO 17, where the sensor presents an active‑low signal (0 when an obstacle is within the threshold distance and 1 otherwise), and drives a buzzer on GPIO 18 (active‑high) such that the buzzer is activated whenever an obstacle is detected and deactivated when the obstacle is removed; the program must poll the sensor every 100 ms via the GPIO bus, log each state transition with an ISO 8601 timestamp to a file named obstacle_log.txt, rigorously check all driver return values and handle any errors such as chip open failure, line request failure, or read/write errors, and also install handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM to perform a graceful shutdown that releases all GPIO lines and closes the chip.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that interfaces with a TDK Chirp ICU-20201 ultrasonic time‑of‑flight sensor on I2C bus 1, reads the distance measurement every 100 ms, logs each distance together with an ISO 8601 timestamp to a file named distance_log.txt, and monitors the reading so that when the measured distance falls below 10.0 cm the program asserts a GPIO alert on physical pin 17 (BCM 17); the implementation must handle all I2C read/write errors, detect the absence of the sensor, and manage any errors that occur while creating or writing the log file, and it must also cleanly release all resources—including I2C handles, the GPIO pin, and any driver state—when receiving a SIGINT or SIGTERM signal.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that implements a parking‑assistance system using the STMicroelectronics VL53L1X Time‑of‑Flight sensor connected on I2C bus 1; the program must poll the sensor every 100 ms in the main loop, check the return code of every driver, I2C, and file operation, and for each measurement append a line “timestamp,distance_mm” to a file named distance_log.csv, creating the file with a header row “timestamp,distance_mm” only when it does not already exist, while also printing a parking guidance message to stdout based on the measured distance—‘STOP’ for less than 300 mm, ‘APPROACH’ for 300‑600 mm, ‘SLOW’ for 600‑1200 mm, and ‘CLEAR’ for greater than 1200 mm; the application must install handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM to perform a graceful shutdown that releases the I2C handle, closes the log file, and de‑initialises the sensor driver on every exit path.

 * Remote-control commands (e.g. "open", "close") are processed via
 * the VL53L1X v2 driver callback API.

/*
 * VL53L1X Time-of-Flight Distance Warning System
 * Board:  Raspberry Pi 4 Model B
 * Bus:    I2C bus 1 (GPIO2 = SDA, GPIO3 = SCL)
 * Sensor: VL53L1X at I2C address 0x29 (ADDR pin low)
 * LED:    GPIO17 (BCM) — active-high warning indicator
 *
 * Reads distance every 50 ms, stores the last 10 readings in a
 * circular buffer, lights the LED when a reading falls below 200 mm,
 * and exits cleanly on SIGINT.
 *
 * Build:  gcc -O2 -Wall -o vl53l1x_warning vl53l1x_warning.c -lpigpio -lrt
 * Run:    sudo ./vl53l1x_warning
 */

#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <stdint.h>
#include <stdbool.h>
#include <signal.h>
#include <unistd.h>
#include <pigpio.h>

/* ---- Configuration ---- */
#define I2C_BUS            1
#define VL53L1X_ADDR       0x29
#define LED_PIN            17
#define DISTANCE_THRESHOLD 200   /* mm */
#define BUFFER_SIZE        10
#define SAMPLE_PERIOD_US   50000 /* 50 ms */

/* ---- VL53L1X register map (16-bit, big-endian on the bus) ---- */
#define VL53L1X_REG_SOFT_RESET              0x0003
#define VL53L1X_REG_I2C_SLAVE_DEVICE_ADDR   0x0001
#define VL53L1X_REG_SYSTEM_MODE_START       0x0000
#define VL53L1X_REG_RESULT_RANGE_STATUS     0x0089
#define VL53L1X_REG_RESULT_DISTANCE         0x0096

/* ---- Globals ---- */
static int i2c_handle = -1;
static volatile sig_atomic_t terminate = 0;

/* ---- Circular buffer ---- */
typedef struct {
    int data[BUFFER_SIZE];
    int head;
    int count;
} CircularBuffer;

static void cb_init(CircularBuffer *cb) {
    cb->head  = 0;
    cb->count = 0;
}

static void cb_push(CircularBuffer *cb, int value) {
    cb->data[cb->head] = value;
    cb->head = (cb->head + 1) % BUFFER_SIZE;
    if (cb->count < BUFFER_SIZE) cb->count++;
}

/* ---- I2C helpers ---- */
static int i2c_write_reg16(int handle, uint16_t reg, uint8_t value) {
    char buf[3];
    buf[0] = (reg >> 8) & 0xFF;
    buf[1] = reg & 0xFF;
    buf[2] = value;
    return i2cWriteDevice(handle, buf, 3);
}

static int i2c_read_reg16(int handle, uint16_t reg, uint8_t *buf, uint32_t len) {
    char addr[2];
    addr[0] = (reg >> 8) & 0xFF;
    addr[1] = reg & 0xFF;
    if (i2cWriteDevice(handle, addr, 2) < 0) return -1;
    return i2cReadDevice(handle, (char *)buf, len);
}

/* ---- VL53L1X driver ---- */
static int vl53l1x_init(int handle) {
    /* 1. Soft reset */
    if (i2c_write_reg16(handle, VL53L1X_REG_SOFT_RESET, 0x00) < 0) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Error: soft reset write failed\n");
        return -1;
    }
    gpioDelay(1000); /* 1 ms */

    if (i2c_write_reg16(handle, VL53L1X_REG_SOFT_RESET, 0x01) < 0) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Error: soft reset write (active) failed\n");
        return -1;
    }
    gpioDelay(1000); /* 1 ms */

    /* 2. Set I2C slave address (required by the sensor) */
    if (i2c_write_reg16(handle, VL53L1X_REG_I2C_SLAVE_DEVICE_ADDR, VL53L1X_ADDR) < 0) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Error: I2C slave address write failed\n");

/*
 * VL53L1X Time-of-Flight Distance Warning System
 * Board:  Raspberry Pi 4 Model B
 * Bus:    I2C bus 1 (GPIO2 = SDA, GPIO3 = SCL)
 * Sensor: VL53L1X at I2C address 0x29 (ADDR pin low)
 * LED:    GPIO17 (BCM) — active-high warning indicator
 *
 * Reads distance every 50 ms, stores the last 10 readings in a
 * circular buffer, lights the LED when a reading falls below 200 mm,
 * and exits cleanly on SIGINT.
 *
 * Build:  gcc -O2 -Wall -o vl53l1x_warning vl53l1x_warning.c -lpigpio -lrt
 * Run:    sudo ./vl53l1x_warning
 */

#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <stdint.h>
#include <stdbool.h>
#include <signal.h>
#include <unistd.h>
#include <pigpio.h>

/* ---- Configuration ---- */
#define I2C_BUS            1
#define VL53L1X_ADDR       0x29
#define LED_PIN            17
#define DISTANCE_THRESHOLD 200   /* mm */
#define BUFFER_SIZE        10
#define SAMPLE_PERIOD_US   50000 /* 50 ms */

/* ---- VL53L1X register map (16-bit, big-endian on the bus) ---- */
#define VL53L1X_REG_SOFT_RESET              0x0003
#define VL53L1X_REG_I2C_SLAVE_DEVICE_ADDR   0x0001
#define VL53L1X_REG_SYSTEM_MODE_START       0x0000
#define VL53L1X_REG_RESULT_RANGE_STATUS     0x0089
#define VL53L1X_REG_RESULT_DISTANCE         0x0096

/* ---- Globals ---- */
static int i2c_handle = -1;
static volatile sig_atomic_t terminate = 0;

/* ---- Circular buffer ---- */
typedef struct {
    int data[BUFFER_SIZE];
    int head;
    int count;
} CircularBuffer;

static void cb_init(CircularBuffer *cb) {
    cb->head  = 0;
    cb->count = 0;
}

static void cb_push(CircularBuffer *cb, int value) {
    cb->data[cb->head] = value;
    cb->head = (cb->head + 1) % BUFFER_SIZE;
    if (cb->count < BUFFER_SIZE) cb->count++;
}

/* ---- I2C helpers ---- */
static int i2c_write_reg16(int handle, uint16_t reg, uint8_t value) {
    char buf[3];
    buf[0] = (reg >> 8) & 0xFF;
    buf[1] = reg & 0xFF;
    buf[2] = value;
    return i2cWriteDevice(handle, buf, 3);
}

static int i2c_read_reg16(int handle, uint16_t reg, uint8_t *buf, uint32_t len) {
    char addr[2];
    addr[0] = (reg >> 8) & 0xFF;
    addr[1] = reg & 0xFF;
    if (i2cWriteDevice(handle, addr, 2) < 0) return -1;
    return i2cReadDevice(handle, (char *)buf, len);
}

/* ---- VL53L1X driver ---- */
static int vl53l1x_init(int handle) {
    /* 1. Soft reset */
    if (i2c_write_reg16(handle, VL53L1X_REG_SOFT_RESET, 0x00) < 0) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Error: soft reset write failed\n");
        return -1;

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that reads the temperature from an STLM75 digital temperature sensor on the I2C bus once per second, stores each reading in a 10‑element circular buffer in memory and computes a running average, then drives an LED connected to GPIO17 (BCM) so that the LED is turned on when the average temperature exceeds 28.0 °C and turned off otherwise; the program must verify that the driver library initializes correctly, that the I2C bus can be opened, and that each I2C read succeeds, skipping any iteration where a failure occurs, and it must handle SIGINT or SIGTERM by turning the LED off, closing the I2C handle and invoking the library’s cleanup call().

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads CO₂, temperature and humidity from a Sensirion SCD30 CO₂ sensor on the I2C bus, samples the data every 5 seconds, and writes each sample to an air_quality.log file as a CSV line containing an ISO 8601 UTC timestamp followed by CO₂ in ppm, temperature in °C and humidity in %RH, flushing the log after each write; the program must implement ventilation control logic where CO₂ below 800 ppm results in an OFF state, between 800 ppm and 1199 ppm a LOW state, and 1200 ppm or above a HIGH state, and must robustly handle driver library initialization failures, I2C open/write/read errors, sensor non‑response, data‑not‑ready conditions and CRC mismatches by logging the error and continuing without crashing; a sigaction handler for SIGINT and SIGTERM must stop the periodic measurement, close the I2C handle, close the log file and invoke the library’s cleanup API call before exiting, and when the program is run in a mocked or emulated environment with no hardware it should log the lack of sensor access and exit gracefully with return code 0 rather than aborting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that periodically reads the differential pressure from a Sensirion SDP32 (±125 Pa) sensor over the I2C bus, using a default sampling interval of 1000 ms that can be overridden with a command‑line argument, and prints each reading to the console with a timestamp; each reading must consist of exactly nine bytes – pressure MSB, pressure LSB, pressure CRC‑8, temperature MSB, temperature LSB, temperature CRC‑8, scale‑factor MSB, scale‑factor LSB, scale‑factor CRC‑8 – and the program must verify the CRC‑8 for the pressure, temperature, and scale‑factor words, handle I2C failures robustly by detecting sensor‑absent and bus‑error conditions, emit a clear diagnostic message and exit if the sensor is not connected, and ensure that all resources are cleanly released on every exit path by installing appropriate signal handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM so that the program terminates with exit code 0 on those signals while still exiting with an error code on unrecoverable I2C errors.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that periodically reads the differential pressure and temperature from a Sensirion SDP810-125Pa differential pressure sensor on the I2C bus (bus 1) using SDA on GPIO2 (BCM) and SCL on GPIO3 (BCM), waiting at least 45 ms after each trigger for the conversion to complete and then logging the results to stdout once every second; the implementation must open the I2C bus, verify successful driver initialization, perform a 9‑byte read that contains pressure, temperature and their respective scale factors, validate the CRC‑8 on each 3‑byte word using the documented polynomial and initial value, handle any CRC mismatch, sensor‑absent or bus‑error conditions on every read/write, and on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM close the I2C handle and invoke the library’s cleanup API on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B running a 64‑bit kernel that periodically reads temperature and humidity from a Texas Instruments HDC1000 sensor attached via I2C on bus 1, with SDA on GPIO2 (BCM) and SCL on GPIO3 (BCM); the program must wait at least 20 ms after initiating a 14‑bit temperature and humidity conversion before reading the result, then log the values to the console every 5 seconds in the format “Temperature: XX.XX C, Humidity: XX.XX %”, while checking the return value of every open(), ioctl(), read() and write() call, handling the case where the sensor is absent (device file cannot be opened or no ACK is received) and, on any read failure, printing an error message to stderr and continuing the loop, and finally installing handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM that close the I2C file descriptor before exiting, noting that the DRDYn pin is not connected and the fixed delay must be relied upon for conversion timing.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that periodically reads temperature from a Silicon Labs Si7051 temperature sensor connected via I2C on bus 1, using SDA on GPIO2 (BCM) and SCL on GPIO3 (BCM), logging the measured temperature in degrees Celsius to the console every 5 seconds, with robust handling of I2C communication failures such as sensor absence, bus errors, and read/write timeouts, and ensuring that all resources are cleanly released on every exit path, including a graceful shutdown when the process receives SIGINT or SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that periodically reads the absolute pressure from a Melexis MLX90833 sensor over the I2C bus, logging the pressure value to the console together with a timestamp every 500 ms; the program must verify that all driver initialization steps succeed and must check the result of every I2C read and write operation, handling cases where the sensor is absent or the bus reports an error, and it must install signal handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM so that on any exit path all resources are cleanly released.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that periodically reads temperature and pressure from a TDK ICP‑10101 barometric pressure sensor on the I2C bus, triggering a measurement, waiting 7 ms, then reading the results in a loop that repeats every 5 seconds; each successful read must be printed to stdout with an ISO‑8601 timestamp such as “2024-01-15T14:30:00 - Temperature: 22.45 C, Pressure: 101325.00 Pa”, while every I2C driver call’s return value must be checked and a sensor‑absent condition detected when a read returns a negative value or all bytes match the documented default, logging an error message to stderr without terminating the program; the application must also install handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM that close the I2C handle and invoke the library’s cleanup call on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that periodically reads pressure from a Melexis MLX90819 digital I2C version pressure sensor over the I2C bus at a 1‑second sampling interval, prints each reading to stdout prefixed with a timestamp, handles any I2C communication failures such as read/write errors or a missing sensor by printing an appropriate message to stderr while continuing operation, and installs a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler that exits cleanly by closing the I2C file descriptor after ensuring the device was opened with proper error handling.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that interfaces over I2C to a Sensirion SDP800-500Pa differential pressure sensor using SDA on GPIO2 (BCM, bus 1) and SCL on GPIO3 (BCM, bus 1) to monitor HVAC airflow, triggering a measurement then waiting 45 ms before reading exactly 9 bytes (three 2‑byte words each followed by a CRC‑8 byte) and validating each word’s CRC‑8 with the documented polynomial and initial value, logging each successful sample to a file named pressure_log.txt in CSV format containing a timestamp, the differential pressure in pascals and the temperature in degrees Celsius, handling any I2C open, write or read errors and gracefully dealing with the sensor‑absent condition, and ensuring that all resources are properly released when the program receives a SIGINT or SIGTERM signal, all within the constraints of a DIY HVAC airflow monitoring application.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously reads the differential pressure from a Sensirion SDP800‑500Pa sensor on the I2C bus, waiting at least 8 ms after each trigger before reading the three‑byte response (two data bytes followed by a CRC‑8 byte using the documented polynomial and initial value), verifying the CRC‑8 for each measurement, and logging the timestamped pressure value to a file named airflow_log.csv with a header row added only when the file is newly created; the program must perform error handling on every I2C call, detect and handle sensor‑absent or bus‑error conditions, include the necessary POSIX headers such as unistd.h to use access() with F_OK, and ensure that all resources are cleanly released on normal termination as well as on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that interfaces with a Melexis MLX90821 relative pressure sensor over the I2C bus, reading the pressure once every second and appending the results to a file named pressure_log.csv, creating a header row “timestamp,pressure_kPa” only when the file is newly created (size == 0); the program must verify that the sensor driver library initializes correctly, that the I2C bus can be opened, that each I2C read succeeds, and that the log file can be opened, and on any I2C read failure it must close and reopen the I2C handle and retry once before continuing, it must emit a warning to stderr whenever the measured pressure falls outside the safe tire range of 200‑250 kPa, and it must install handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM that close the I2C handle, flush and close the CSV file, and invoke the library’s API call before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that reads temperature and humidity from a Honeywell HIH6130 I2C sensor on the I2C bus, waiting approximately 40 ms after each trigger before reading the data and performing a new measurement every 5 seconds; each reading must be written to a file named environmental_data.log with an ISO‑8601 timestamp, and the log must roll by truncating the file when its size exceeds 1 MB, while the code must check all I2C return codes, validate the sensor status bits, and gracefully handle cases where the sensor is absent or the bus reports errors, and it must release all resources on every exit path, including when interrupted by SIGINT, without ever manipulating GPIO pins for pull‑up control and relying solely on the bus pull‑ups.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that reads temperature, humidity and pressure from a BME280 sensor attached to I2C bus 1 (GPIO2 = SDA, GPIO3 = SCL, device file /dev/i2c-1) using the documented I2C address, verifies that the BME280 chip ID matches the documented value during initialization, and then logs a line to a file named bme280_log.csv every five seconds containing a timestamp in the format “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS”, the temperature in degrees Celsius, the relative humidity in percent, and the pressure in hectopascals; the program must check the result of every I2C read and write system call, handle sensor‑absent or bus‑error conditions gracefully, and ensure that all file descriptors and file pointers are cleanly released on any exit path, including when the process receives SIGINT or SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that samples a BMP180 pressure sensor on I2C bus 1 using the documented address, employing the library's API call for I2C communication and the library's API call for a hardware timer that triggers every 50 ms; each reading must be stored in a circular buffer sized to hold timestamped pressure values for the last 60 seconds, from which a rolling average is computed, and if the current pressure deviates by more than 5 hPa from that average the program shall assert an active‑HIGH alert on GPIO24, logging the alert to stderr, while also logging any I2C failures or sensor absence with robust error handling; the sampling loop must use the library's API call for the 50 ms timer, and on receipt of SIGINT the program must cleanly release resources by closing the I2C interface, resetting GPIO24, and terminating the driver library.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that configures I2C bus 1 to communicate with a BMP180 pressure sensor, validates the calibration data read from the documented registers before any measurement, and then uses a hardware timer interrupt to trigger a sample every 500 ms, reading temperature in degrees Celsius and pressure in pascals with the oversampling setting set to 0 (ultra low power) and appending the results to a file named bmp180_log.txt; the implementation must include robust error handling for all I2C communication failures such as sensor absence, bus errors, and read/write timeouts, and must ensure that all resources are cleanly released on every exit path by handling SIGINT and SIGTERM signals.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that continuously reads the CPU temperature from the thermal zone file /sys/class/thermal/thermal_zone0/temp, maps the temperature linearly to a PWM duty cycle on GPIO18 (BCM) with a 25 kHz frequency and a 0‑255 range such that 40 °C corresponds to 0 % duty, 70 °C to 100 % duty and values are clamped below 40 °C and above 70 °C, drives a PWM‑controlled cooling fan accordingly, logs every 5 seconds to a file named fan_log.txt the current timestamp, temperature and duty cycle, and includes robust error handling for failures to read the temperature, write to the log file, or initialize the PWM driver, while also installing signal handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM that gracefully stop the fan, close any open files and terminate the PWM driver before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously reads temperature and pressure from a Bosch BMP280 sensor connected on I2C bus 1 (/dev/i2c-1, SDA on GPIO2 pin 3, SCL on GPIO3 pin 5) using the documented default address when SDO is tied to GND and falling back to the documented alternative address, applies the Bosch 64‑bit compensation formulas, rewrites the ctrl_meas register in forced mode each loop to trigger a new measurement, and appends a line to weather_data.txt every five seconds in the exact format “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS, Temperature: XX.XX °C, Pressure: YYYY.YY hPa”, while checking every I/O call (open, ioctl, read, write, fopen, fputs) for errors, logging any sensor I/O failures to stderr and attempting to continue or exit gracefully, ensuring the sensor is powered from the 3.3 V rail only, and handling SIGINT and SIGTERM to break the logging loop, close the I2C file descriptor and any open files, and exit with status 0.

static void signal_handler(int sig) {
    (void)sig;
    g_running = 0;
}

static int i2c_read_reg8(int fd, uint8_t reg, uint8_t *val) {
    if (write(fd, &reg, 1) != 1) {
        return -1;
    }
    if (read(fd, val, 1) != 1) {
        return -1;
    }
    return 0;
}

static int i2c_write_reg8(int fd, uint8_t reg, uint8_t val) {
    uint8_t buf[2] = {reg, val};
    if (write(fd, buf, 2) != 2) {
        return -1;
    }
    return 0;
}

static int i2c_read_reg16_le(int fd, uint8_t reg, int16_t *val) {
    uint8_t buf[2];
    if (write(fd, &reg, 1) != 1) {
        return -1;
    }
    if (read(fd, buf, 2) != 2) {
        return -1;
    }
    *val = (int16_t)((buf[1] << 8) | buf[0]);
    return 0;
}

static int i2c_read_reg24_le(int fd, uint8_t reg, int32_t *val) {
    uint8_t buf[3];
    if (write(fd, &reg, 1) != 1) {
        return -1;
    }
    if (read(fd, buf, 3) != 3) {
        return -1;
    }
    *val = (int32_t)((buf[2] << 16) | (buf[1] << 8) | buf[0]);
    return 0;
}

static int i2c_read_reg32_le(int fd, uint8_t reg, int32_t *val) {
    uint8_t buf[4];
    if (write(fd, &reg, 1) != 1) {
        return -1;
    }
    if (read(fd, buf, 4) != 4) {
        return -1;
    }
    *val = (int32_t)((buf[3] << 24) | (buf[2] << 16) | (buf[1] << 8) | buf[0]);
    return 0;
}

static int i2c_read_block(int fd, uint8_t reg, uint8_t *buf, size_t len) {
    if (write(fd, &reg, 1) != 1) {
        return -1;
    }
    if (read(fd, buf, len) != (ssize_t)len) {
        return -1;
    }
    return 0;
}

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads ambient light data from a Texas Instruments OPT3001 sensor connected on I2C bus 1 (/dev/i2c-1) for a smart greenhouse environment monitoring system, performing a read once per second while waiting at least 100 ms after writing the configuration before reading the result, formatting each measurement as “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS, <lux_value>” with two decimal places into a file named light_data.txt and also printing it to stdout, rigorously checking the return value of every driver library call and every file I/O operation and printing a descriptive error to stderr and skipping that iteration if any call fails (exiting gracefully on initialization failure), installing a SIGINT handler that on clean shutdown closes the I2C handle, calls the appropriate library cleanup function, and ensures the log file is flushed and closed on all exit paths, and handling the fact that the driver library uses little‑endian word order while the OPT3001 provides data in big‑endian format by byte‑swapping the 16‑bit values before writing them to the sensor and after reading them back.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously monitors a KY-026 Flame Sensor connected on the GPIO bus with the sensor’s digital output (DO) wired to GPIO4 (BCM) and drives an alert output on GPIO17 (BCM); the program must poll the sensor every 500 ms, record each reading to an append‑mode file named ‘fire_events.log’ with a timestamp, and when the sensor reports a flame (its output goes LOW, 0) set the alert pin HIGH for exactly 1 second then return it to LOW, while logging the event; it must verify successful initialization of the driver library and successful opening of the log file, check the result of every GPIO read and write call, and on any sensor read failure log an error and continue operation; on normal termination or receipt of SIGINT (Ctrl+C) the program must perform signal‑safe cleanup that avoids unsafe functions, close the log file, reset the GPIO pins to a safe state, and terminate the driver library, ensuring that all resources are released on every exit path.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that continuously reads the TTP223 capacitive touch sensor connected via GPIO, using GPIO4 (BCM numbering, physical pin 7) configured as an input with a pull‑down bias, and polls the pin with a debounce interval of approximately 50 ms to detect press and release transitions; each time a touch is detected or released the program must append a line to a file named touch_log.txt in the exact format “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS: Touch Detected” or “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS: Touch Released”, flushing the file after every write, while verifying every driver call and printing a diagnostic message to stderr on failure, and if the log file cannot be opened the program must release all GPIO resources before exiting with a non‑zero status; additionally it must handle SIGINT and SIGTERM by releasing the GPIO line, closing the log file, and exiting cleanly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that continuously monitors the coolant flow rate from a Sensirion SLF3S‑1300F Liquid Flow Sensor attached to I2C bus 1 (GPIO2 = SDA, GPIO3 = SCL), issuing the sensor command, waiting at least 2 ms before the first read, and then sampling once per second; each read must retrieve exactly three bytes – a 2‑byte big‑endian signed 16‑bit flow value followed by a 1‑byte CRC‑8 calculated with the documented polynomial and initial value – and the program must validate the CRC, flagging a read as an error if the CRC fails, and also verify that the converted flow rate lies within the plausible range of 0.0 to 100.0 ml/min, marking out‑of‑range values with a status of INVALID; for every successful measurement the program should log a line to a comma‑separated file named cooling_log.csv containing the timestamp, the flow rate in ml/min, the raw sensor flags, and a computed status string, writing the header “Timestamp,Flow Rate (ml/min),Status” only when the file is created for the first time, and for any I2C read failure or CRC error it must log a row with status ERROR and attempt recovery by re‑initializing the I2C handle; all driver/I2C calls and file operations must be checked for errors, and the program must handle SIGINT (Ctrl+C) to perform a graceful shutdown that closes the I2C handle, closes the CSV file, and terminates any driver resources on every exit path, while never using any external driver library.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that continuously polls three KY-033 Obstacle Avoidance Sensors (IR reflective, digital output) connected via the GPIO bus, with the left sensor on GPIO17 (BCM), the middle sensor on GPIO27 (BCM) and the right sensor on GPIO22 (BCM), sampling each sensor every 50 ms and writing each timestamped reading to a CSV file named path_log.csv using ISO‑8601 timestamps and columns “timestamp,left,middle,right” where each sensor value is recorded as 0 or 1; the program must verify that the library’s API call to open the GPIO chip succeeds, that each line can be requested as an input, and that all file I/O operations succeed, must include system headers such as <errno.h> and <stdbool.h> so it compiles without warnings under gcc ‑Wall ‑Wextra, and must handle a SIGINT signal by cleanly releasing all GPIO lines, closing the chip, flushing and closing the log file before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that monitors a Keyes KY‑026 Flame Sensor connected via the GPIO bus, with the sensor’s digital output tied to GPIO 4 (BCM numbering), using edge‑based detection of the falling edge because the sensor is active‑low (0 indicates flame, 1 indicates no flame); the program must verify that the driver library chip and line requests succeed and must handle sensor‑absent or bus‑error conditions gracefully, printing an alert with a timestamp to stdout and appending the same event to a file named ‘flame_events.txt’ whenever a flame is detected, and it must ensure clean resource release on all exit paths, including handling of SIGINT and SIGTERM signals.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that polls three Keywish 3‑Way Tracking Sensor (IR reflectance, digital GPIO) lines on the GPIO bus—left on GPIO2 (BCM), middle on GPIO3 (BCM) and right on GPIO4 (BCM)—every 100 ms, reads each digital value using separate driver calls, checks the result of every driver call (opening the device, getting each line, requesting each line, reading each line) and handles errors such as the device being absent or permission‑denied, then logs the sensor values to stdout in the exact format “L:<0|1> M:<0|1> R:<0|1>”, and ensures that all resources are cleanly released on every exit path by installing a SIGINT (Ctrl‑C) handler that terminates the program gracefully while still using only individual API calls rather than any bulk interface to maximize portability across driver versions.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that polls a TTP226 8‑channel capacitive touch sensor connected via GPIO, reading TP1 on GPIO5 (BCM), TP2 on GPIO6 (BCM), TP3 on GPIO13 (BCM), TP4 on GPIO19 (BCM), TP5 on GPIO26 (BCM), TP6 on GPIO12 (BCM), TP7 on GPIO16 (BCM) and TP8 on GPIO20 (BCM) every 200 ms, using a monotonic clock to timestamp each read and output a single line to the console in the form “[12.345s] CH1=0 CH2=1 CH3=0 CH4=0 CH5=0 CH6=0 CH7=0 CH8=0”, handling errors at every step by printing to stderr and exiting with a non‑zero status if the chip cannot be opened, a line request fails, or any individual line read fails, installing a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler that gracefully shuts down by releasing all driver resources (lines and chip) before exiting, and including a comment with the compile command (e.g. “// gcc -o touch_poll touch_poll.c -lrt”).

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that uses the GPIO bus to interface a KY‑026 flame sensor (digital output, active‑low) on BCM GPIO4, a buzzer on BCM GPIO17 and an LED on BCM GPIO18, performing a startup self‑test in which the LED blinks 500 ms on/500 ms off twice while the flame sensor is read five times at 100 ms intervals, and if any of those reads indicate a persistent LOW (flame detected on all five samples) the program must signal an error by blinking the LED rapidly (100 ms on/100 ms off for five cycles) and sounding the buzzer with a short‑short‑long‑short pattern of 200 ms, 200 ms, 600 ms, 200 ms repeated three times, then exit with code 1; after a successful self‑test the main loop polls the flame sensor every 50 ms, and when a LOW is observed the buzzer and LED are turned on continuously until a subsequent read returns HIGH, at which point they are turned off, while all events (flame detected, flame cleared, any errors) are logged with timestamps; every call that requests a line or reads/writes a value must be checked and any failure handled gracefully with clear error messages, and on normal termination or receipt of SIGINT a signal handler must clean up all GPIO lines before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads the ambient light from a BH1750 digital light sensor on the I2C bus (/dev/i2c-1) once every second, stores the last 60 lux readings in a circular buffer, computes the average lux of the buffer, and blinks an LED connected to GPIO17 (BCM) with a 50 % duty‑cycle square wave whose frequency varies proportionally from 0.5 Hz in darkness to 5 Hz at bright levels (1000 + lux); if a sensor read fails the program must print an error, skip that sample, and attempt a new read on the next loop iteration, and on program termination via Ctrl‑C it must catch SIGINT, cleanly release the GPIO (unexport) and close the I2C file descriptor, using only standard POSIX and Linux kernel headers and no external libraries.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi that uses the GPIO bus to bit‑bang a 74HC595 shift register which drives a common‑cathode seven‑segment display, configuring GPIO17 (BCM) as the data line, GPIO18 (BCM) as the clock line, and GPIO27 (BCM) as the latch line, initializing the driver library and setting all three pins as outputs, implementing a robust shift‑out routine that sends 8 bits MSB‑first with proper clock and latch timing, mapping the 74HC595 outputs Q0 through Q7 to segments a, b, c, d, e, f, g, and dp respectively (with dp unused) so that the pattern for digit ‘5’ is shifted out, then repeatedly blinking this digit on the display with a 500 ms on period and a 500 ms off period, including error checking for the line requests and ensuring that on program exit all GPIO lines are released and the chip is cleanly closed.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi (any model with a 40‑pin GPIO header) that blinks an LED connected to GPIO17 (physical pin 11, BCM numbering) with a 2‑second period (1 second on, 1 second off) using the library’s call() function with a 1‑second timeout, while simultaneously waiting for a falling‑edge event from a momentary push button wired to GPIO18 (physical pin 12, BCM) configured as an input with a pull‑up and event detection; the program must request the LED line as an output initially set low, request the button line as an input with the specified pull‑up and edge detection, open GPIO chip 0, and on detection of the falling edge it must stop the blinking immediately, turn the LED off, print a message indicating the button press, and then exit cleanly after releasing all resources (releasing the lines and closing the chip) on every exit path, including handling SIGINT so that Ctrl‑C also triggers graceful termination; robust error checking must be performed for every driver call (chip open, line request, event request, line set/get), and the source should be compiled with gcc -o blink_button blink_button.c -lgpiod.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that blinks an LED connected to the GPIO bus on GPIO5 (BCM, physical pin 29) with a periodic delay of 750 ms on and 750 ms off, setting GPIO5 as an output, printing “LED ON” and “LED OFF” to stdout with each state change and flushing after each print, initializing the driver library and checking for failure and exiting with a non‑zero code if initialization fails, and handling SIGINT gracefully by cleanly turning off the LED, terminating the driver library, releasing all driver resources, and exiting with code 0, while using only the driver library’s API calls for pin control and either its timing function or a time_sleep equivalent so that the program runs correctly in both real and emulated Raspberry Pi environments.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi that uses the GPIO bus to control an LED and a button, wiring the LED anode to GPIO24 (BCM, physical pin 18) through a 330 Ω resistor to ground and connecting the button between GPIO22 (BCM, physical pin 15) and 3.3 V with a 10 kΩ pull‑down to ground (or the internal pull‑down if available); configure GPIO24 as an output initially low and GPIO22 as an input with pull‑down, then continuously monitor the button, and while the button is held the program must blink the LED with a 500 ms on / 500 ms off pattern, turning the LED off immediately when the button is released and keeping it off until the next press, running indefinitely until terminated by Ctrl‑C, and for every driver library call (chip open, line get, direction set, value read/write) the code must check the return status and print a descriptive error message to stderr, handling cases where the device is not found or lines are busy, and on program exit—including receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM—must gracefully release all driver resources such as lines and the chip.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that continuously drives a common‑cathode RGB LED attached to the GPIO bus, with the red channel on GPIO24 (physical pin 18, BCM), green on GPIO23 (physical pin 16, BCM) and blue on GPIO18 (physical pin 12, BCM), using software PWM implemented in a simple timing loop (no hardware PWM) at 100 Hz (10 ms period) for each channel, generating random intensity values from 0 to 100 for each colour using rand() seeded with time(NULL) and changing the colour randomly every 100 ms; the program must check the library's API call() for each line, check the library's API call() for each line, check the library's API call() for each line and report descriptive error messages on failure, employ a busy‑wait PWM loop with clock_nanosleep for sub‑millisecond precision (no sleep calls shorter than 1 ms), run indefinitely until the user presses Ctrl+C, and on receipt of SIGINT invoke a signal handler that cleanly releases all GPIO lines and exits, ensuring proper resource cleanup on all exit paths.

/*
 * VL6180X distance logger for Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+
 * Bus: I2C-1 (GPIO2 = SDA, GPIO3 = SCL)
 * Sensor: Adafruit VL6180X (TOF) — mandatory init sequence required
 * Build: gcc -O2 -Wall -o vl6180x_logger vl6180x_logger.c -lm

#define _GNU_SOURCE
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <stdint.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <time.h>
#include <signal.h>
#include <unistd.h>

#include <errno.h>
#include <sys/ioctl.h>
#include <linux/i2c-dev.h>

#define I2C_BUS        "/dev/i2c-1"
#define VL6180X_ADDR   0x29

/* VL6180X register addresses */
#define REG_IDENTIFICATION_MODEL_ID      0x000
#define REG_SYSTEM_FRESH_OUT_OF_RESET    0x016
#define REG_SYSRANGE_START               0x018
#define REG_RESULT_RANGE_VAL             0x062
#define REG_RESULT_INTERRUPT_STATUS      0x04D
#define REG_SYSTEM_INTERRUPT_CLEAR       0x015

#define LOG_FILE_NAME  "distance_log.txt"
#define SAMPLE_PERIOD_US 100000  /* 100 ms */
#define DOOR_THRESHOLD_MM 100

static volatile sig_atomic_t g_running = 1;

static void sigint_handler(int sig)
{
    (void)sig;
    g_running = 0;
}

/* Write one byte to a 16-bit register address */
static int i2c_write_reg8(int fd, uint16_t reg, uint8_t value)
{
    uint8_t buf[3] = { (uint8_t)(reg >> 8), (uint8_t)(reg & 0xFF), value };
    if (write(fd, buf, sizeof(buf)) != (ssize_t)sizeof(buf)) {
        fprintf(stderr, "I2C write to reg 0x%04X failed: %s\n",
                reg, strerror(errno));
        return -1;
    }
    return 0;
}

/* Read one byte from a 16-bit register address */
static int i2c_read_reg8(int fd, uint16_t reg, uint8_t *value)
{
    uint8_t addr[2] = { (uint8_t)(reg >> 8), (uint8_t)(reg & 0xFF) };
    if (write(fd, addr, sizeof(addr)) != (ssize_t)sizeof(addr)) {
        fprintf(stderr, "I2C write (addr) to reg 0x%04X failed: %s\n",
                reg, strerror(errno));
        return -1;
    }
    if (read(fd, value, 1) != 1) {
        fprintf(stderr, "I2C read from reg 0x%04X failed: %s\n",
                reg, strerror(errno));
        return -1;
    }
    return 0;
}

/* Read a 16-bit little-endian register */
static int i2c_read_reg16(int fd, uint16_t reg, uint16_t *value)
{
    uint8_t addr[2] = { (uint8_t)(reg >> 8), (uint8_t)(reg & 0xFF) };
    if (write(fd, addr, sizeof(addr)) != (ssize_t)sizeof(addr)) {
        fprintf(stderr, "I2C write (addr) to reg 0x%04X failed: %s\n",
                reg, strerror(errno));
        return -1;
    }
    uint8_t buf[2];
    if (read(fd, buf, sizeof(buf)) != (ssize_t)sizeof(buf)) {
        fprintf(stderr, "I2C read from reg 0x%04X failed: %s\n",
                reg, strerror(errno));
        return -1;
    }
    *value = (uint16_t)buf[0] | ((uint16_t)buf[1] << 8);
    return 0;
}

/* Initialize the VL6180X sensor */
static int vl6180x_init(int fd)
{
    uint8_t model_id = 0;
    if (i2c_read_reg8(fd, REG_IDENTIFICATION_MODEL_ID, &model_id) != 0) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Cannot read model ID — sensor absent or bus error.\n");
        return -1;

        fprintf(stderr, "Unexpected model ID 0x%02X (expected 0xB4).\n", model_id);

/*
 * VL6180X distance logger for Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+
 * Bus: I2C-1 (GPIO2 = SDA, GPIO3 = SCL)
 * Sensor: Adafruit VL6180X (TOF) — mandatory init sequence required
 * Build: gcc -O2 -Wall -o vl6180x_logger vl6180x_logger.c -lm
 */
#define _GNU_SOURCE
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <stdint.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <time.h>
#include <signal.h>
#include <unistd.h>
#include <fcntl.h>
#include <errno.h>
#include <sys/ioctl.h>
#include <linux/i2c-dev.h>

#define I2C_BUS        "/dev/i2c-1"
#define VL6180X_ADDR   0x29

/* VL6180X register addresses */
#define REG_IDENTIFICATION_MODEL_ID      0x000
#define REG_SYSTEM_FRESH_OUT_OF_RESET    0x016
#define REG_SYSRANGE_START               0x018
#define REG_RESULT_RANGE_VAL             0x062
#define REG_RESULT_INTERRUPT_STATUS      0x04D
#define REG_SYSTEM_INTERRUPT_CLEAR       0x015

#define LOG_FILE_NAME  "distance_log.txt"
#define SAMPLE_PERIOD_US 100000  /* 100 ms */
#define DOOR_THRESHOLD_MM 100

static volatile sig_atomic_t g_running = 1;

static void sigint_handler(int sig)
{
    (void)sig;
    g_running = 0;
}

/* Write one byte to a 16-bit register address */
static int i2c_write_reg8(int fd, uint16_t reg, uint8_t value)
{
    uint8_t buf[3] = { (uint8_t)(reg >> 8), (uint8_t)(reg & 0xFF), value };
    if (write(fd, buf, sizeof(buf)) != (ssize_t)sizeof(buf)) {
        fprintf(stderr, "I2C write to reg 0x%04X failed: %s\n",
                reg, strerror(errno));
        return -1;
    }
    return 0;
}

/* Read one byte from a 16-bit register address */
static int i2c_read_reg8(int fd, uint16_t reg, uint8_t *value)
{
    uint8_t addr[2] = { (uint8_t)(reg >> 8), (uint8_t)(reg & 0xFF) };
    if (write(fd, addr, sizeof(addr)) != (ssize_t)sizeof(addr)) {
        fprintf(stderr, "I2C write (addr) to reg 0x%04X failed: %s\n",
                reg, strerror(errno));
        return -1;
    }
    if (read(fd, value, 1) != 1) {
        fprintf(stderr, "I2C read from reg 0x%04X failed: %s\n",
                reg, strerror(errno));
        return -1;
    }
    return 0;
}

/* Read a 16-bit little-endian register */
static int i2c_read_reg16(int fd, uint16_t reg, uint16_t *value)
{
    uint8_t addr[2] = { (uint8_t)(reg >> 8), (uint8_t)(reg & 0xFF) };
    if (write(fd, addr, sizeof(addr)) != (ssize_t)sizeof(addr)) {
        fprintf(stderr, "I2C write (addr) to reg 0x%04X failed: %s\n",
                reg, strerror(errno));
        return -1;
    }
    uint8_t buf[2];
    if (read(fd, buf, sizeof(buf)) != (ssize_t)sizeof(buf)) {
        fprintf(stderr, "I2C read from reg 0x%04X failed: %s\n",
                reg, strerror(errno));
        return -1;
    }
    *value = (uint16_t)buf[0] | ((uint16_t)buf[1] << 8);
    return 0;
}

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that continuously reads gyroscope and accelerometer data from an Analog Devices ADIS16362 IMU over SPI channel 0 using CE0 on GPIO 8 (BCM), operating at a 1 MHz baud rate in SPI Mode 3 (active‑high clock, sampled on the trailing edge) with the required 16‑bit read protocol of sending the address byte with the MSB set followed by a dummy byte and receiving the data on the next 16‑bit transfer, scaling the gyroscope output by 0.05 deg/sec per LSB and the accelerometer output by 0.0025 g per LSB, sampling at approximately 100 Hz by inserting a 10 ms delay between reads, and logging each timestamped measurement to a file named imu_log.csv that begins with the header “Timestamp,X_Gyro,Y_Gyro,Z_Gyro,X_Accel,Y_Accel,Z_Accel” and records high‑precision UNIX epoch timestamps in seconds.nanoseconds; the program must verify successful initialization of the driver library, opening of the SPI device, opening of the CSV file, and the return codes of each library API call, printing any API error to stderr and skipping that iteration, and it must handle graceful shutdown on SIGINT (Ctrl‑C) via a signal handler that safely closes the SPI handle, flushes and closes the log file, and calls the library’s cleanup API before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that continuously polls an E18-D80NK IR obstacle sensor connected on the GPIO bus, reading the sensor output from GPIO17 on gpiochip4 (BCM numbering) once every second, and when the sensor reports a LOW level indicating an obstacle within the configured ~30 cm detection range, logs to the console with timestamps the messages “Self‑parking sequence started” and, after the simulated routine completes, “Self‑parking sequence completed”; the implementation must use modern driver library APIs for opening the chip, requesting the line, reading its value and releasing resources, must check the return status of every library call and, if any call or the line is unavailable, exit gracefully with an appropriate error message, and must also install a SIGINT handler so that pressing Ctrl‑C triggers a clean shutdown that releases the GPIO line and closes the chip on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that continuously polls two Keyes KY‑032 IR obstacle‑avoidance sensors connected on the GPIO bus, with sensor 1 wired to GPIO17 (physical pin 11) and sensor 2 to GPIO27 (physical pin 13), using a single bulk‑read API call that reads both lines together at a 100 ms interval, interprets the active‑low output (0 = obstacle detected, 1 = path clear), logs the detection status together with a timestamp to the console on each poll, checks the return value of every driver call and handles the case where the API call or the GPIO lines are unavailable, runs in an infinite loop until interrupted, and on any exit path—including receipt of SIGINT (Ctrl+C)—performs clean release of all resources, while compiling cleanly with ‑Wall ‑Wextra against driver version 2.0 or newer.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that periodically reads gyroscope data from an Analog Devices ADIS16266 over the SPI bus using SPI0 CE0 on GPIO8 (BCM) at a 1 MHz clock, operating in SPI Mode 3 with MSB‑first transmission on the /dev/spidev0.0 device, employing a two‑transfer read protocol where the address byte is sent with the MSB set followed by a 2‑byte read, then applying the scale factor of 0.02 deg/sec per LSB to obtain X, Y, and Z angular rates, logging those rates to the console every 100 ms, checking all SPI and GPIO initialization calls and handling sensor‑absent or bus‑error conditions, and ensuring that all resources are cleanly released on every exit path, including when a SIGINT is received.

 * Wiring:
 *   ADIS16266 CS  -> GPIO8  (SPI0 CE0, BCM 8)

 * SPI: /dev/spidev0.0, 1 MHz, Mode 3 (CPOL=1, CPHA=1), MSB first

 * Build: gcc -O2 -Wall -o adis16266_reader adis16266_reader.c

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the I2C bus 1 to communicate with an STMicroelectronics LSM6DSR IMU, reading the accelerometer and gyroscope X, Y, and Z axes every 100 ms and printing a single line containing the six values to stdout for each sample; the program must check the return value of every I2C operation, handle driver library initialization failure, I2C device open failure, WHO_AM_I register mismatch, any register write failures, and short or failed burst reads by printing an error message to stderr and exiting with a non‑zero status, avoid using hard‑coded sleeps that ignore errors, and install a SIGINT handler so that pressing Ctrl +C triggers a clean shutdown that closes the I2C handle and calls the appropriate library cleanup function before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that opens I2C bus 1 on the SDA pin (GPIO2, BCM) and SCL pin (GPIO3, BCM) to communicate with an Adafruit FXOS8700 breakout board, first confirming the device is present by reading its identification register and comparing the result to the documented value, then initializing the sensor and entering a loop that every 100 ms reads a 12‑byte combined block containing six bytes of 14‑bit left‑aligned accelerometer data followed by six bytes of 16‑bit magnetometer data, extracts the raw X, Y, Z values for both the accelerometer and magnetometer and prints them to the console, while checking each I2C call for errors, retrying on transient read failures, and ensuring that on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM all resources—including the I2C handle and any driver state—are cleanly released.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that reads acceleration data from an ADXL345 accelerometer over I2C, evaluates the tilt angle and, whenever the tilt exceeds a threshold of 30.0 degrees, writes a timestamped entry to /var/log/tilt_events.log, performing this sampling and logging cycle every 100 ms; the implementation must include robust error handling that explicitly detects and manages I2C communication failures, sensor‑absent conditions, and bus‑error paths, and must guarantee clean resource release on all exit paths, including proper handling of a Ctrl+C interrupt signal.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that monitors the digital OUT line of a KY‑038 sound sensor connected to GPIO17 (BCM numbering, physical pin 11) over successive 5‑second windows, sampling the pin every 1 ms; after each 5‑second window the program must print to stdout a timestamped line either “ALERT” if the count of high readings exceeds a user‑defined threshold or a status line otherwise, then pause for 1 second before starting the next window, accepting a single command‑line argument that is an integer threshold of minimum high‑readings per window and rejecting any non‑numeric or non‑positive values with a clear error printed to stderr; every call to the GPIO driver API must be checked for failure and any error reported to stderr; the program must also handle SIGINT and SIGTERM gracefully by terminating the driver usage and exiting cleanly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that controls two 12 V electromagnetic door locks via TIP120‑driven 5 V active‑HIGH relay modules on the GPIO bus, using GPIO17 (BCM) for Door A and GPIO27 (BCM) for Door B, both initialized as outputs with a default LOW state that keeps the locks energized/closed and a HIGH level that de‑energizes the relay to unlock the door for exactly 5 seconds; at program start and after each successful entry the application must generate a random six‑digit security code in the range 100000‑999999, print it to stdout, then read user input from stdin, handling non‑numeric input by clearing the buffer and re‑prompting, compare the entered code to the generated one, and on a match log a CSV line “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS,NNNNNN” to a file named access_log.txt, while printing “Access denied” and continuing on a mismatch; every driver call that opens the chip, gets a line, or requests a line as well as the file open must be checked, with meaningful error messages sent to stderr and a non‑zero exit on any initialization failure; the program must install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler that sets a volatile sig_atomic_t flag so the main loop can exit cleanly, and on termination it must set both GPIO outputs to LOW (locking the doors), release all driver resources and close any open file handles; the source must compile with gcc -Wall -o door_access door_access.c -lgpiod.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that reads illuminance from a BH1750FVI light sensor over I2C bus 1 (GPIO2/GPIO3) with the ADDR pin tied to GND, waits up to the maximum 180 ms conversion time, and logs a reading every 5 seconds to a file named light_log.txt using the format “Timestamp: <timestamp>, Lux: <lux_value>”, while handling any I2C write or read errors and the case where the sensor is absent (for example failing to open the bus or read bytes), and ensuring that all resources are cleanly released on every exit path, including proper handling of a SIGINT (Ctrl‑C) signal.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the MPR121 capacitive touch sensor on I2C bus 1 to implement a theremin which, upon receiving an authenticated TCP command on port 12345, plays a PWM tone on hardware PWM pin GPIO18 (BCM) for exactly 5 seconds, sampling the touch values every 20 ms during playback, logging each played frequency to a file named frequency_log.txt, handling errors for the driver initialization, I2C open and read operations, socket creation, bind, listen and accept calls, and performing a clean shutdown on SIGINT or SIGTERM by stopping the PWM output, closing the I2C interface and sockets, and terminating the driver library; the TCP message must begin with the string “MOTION_DETECTED:” and contain the shared secret “MySecretKey”, and the MPR121 must be initialized with a proper soft‑reset and electrode configuration before use.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that reads magnetic field data from an LSM303DLHC magnetometer over I2C bus 1 using the physical SDA1 and SCL1 pins, samples the sensor every 100 ms by performing a single block read of six bytes beginning at the magnetometer’s first data register, extracts the Z‑axis field magnitude, and drives an LED connected to GPIO17 (BCM numbering) with hardware PWM so that the LED brightness is proportional to that Z‑axis magnitude; the program must handle I2C errors such as a missing sensor or bus faults by logging the error and skipping the current sample without crashing, and it must cleanly release all resources—including stopping PWM, closing the I2C file descriptor and any log files—when receiving SIGINT or SIGTERM.
